sweep_summary: Ten titles searched for viet1252 (catalog: no-word-stress, deciding source Brunelle 2017 JIPA, quotation re-verified in the text we hold). tone/intonation, silent on word stress; only a phrase-boundary remark that demarcative marking falls on the last lexical syllable before extrametrical final particles), Jannedy 2007 ISIS 8 (Potsdam; focus prosody, silent, repeats Thompson's pause-group stress), Ha 2012 A-PL monograph (ANU; intonation of short utterances, silent), and Schiering, Bickel & Hildebrandt 2010 JL (CORE mirror of the ZORA postprint; the published form of the Glottolog 'Does Vietnamese have prosodic words?' talk), which explicitly denies a separate word-stress layer and places stress at the phonological-phrase level — confirms the classification, does not supersede Brunelle 2017. Not obtainable: Henderson 1966 (archive.org lending only; Firthian syllable analysis, low priority), Ingram & Nguyen 2007 MKS 37 (sealang refused connections; medium priority as the main competing experimental work), Nguyen, Ingram & Pensalfini 2008 (paywalled; abstract only, L2 English), Ha 2013 De Gruyter chapter (paywalled; conversation prosody), Lanh 1980 Russian avtoreferat (not found; sentence intonation). Nothing found contradicts the catalog; no reclassification suggested.org, ANU DSpace, Potsdam OPUS and UQ eSpace APIs directly.

new_statements.quote: The acoustic evidence from the production experiments does not support the idea of a separate layer of word stress in Vietnamese. (p.671) ... To summarize, Vietnamese provides ample evidence for a genuine stress domain that is preferably disyllabic and maximally trisyllabic. Within this domain, stress is realized on the final syllable in the default case. Crucially, this domain is computed irrespective of the morphosyntactic status of its constituent syllables, i.e. stress phonology does not distinguish between a word-level and a phrasal-level of prosodic structure. Metrically, polysyllabic words are thus indistinguishable from other combinations of syllables. (p.672)
new_statements.citation: Schiering, René, Balthasar Bickel & Kristine A. Hildebrandt. 2010. The prosodic word is not universal, but emergent. Journal of Linguistics 46(3): 657-709. doi:10.1017/S0022226710000216
new_statements.reading: Vietnamese has no word-level stress: prominence is assigned within a phrase-level stress unit (2-3 syllables, final syllable strong by default, semantic salience overriding), identically for words and phrases; polysyllabic words are metrically indistinguishable from phrases. This is a typological synthesis of Thompson 1965 and the Ingram & Nguyen experiments, not a new instrumental study, and it agrees with the catalog's no-word-stress coding.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction to the bearing. Refinement only: Schiering et al. deny a word-level stress layer but still posit a genuine phrasal stress domain (iambic, final by default, semantic salience overriding, Sino-Vietnamese compounds left-branch), assigning stress to the Phonological Phrase (p.673); Brunelle 2017 goes further and denies stress altogether, reinterpreting final prominence as phrase-final lengthening. Both are consistent with the catalog's no word stress / domain word coding.

new_statements.quote: The results suggested that Vietnamese lacks phonetic resources for distinguishing compounds from phrases lexically and that native speakers may employ a phrase-level prosodic disambiguation strategy (juncture marking), when required to do so. However, in a second series of experiments, minimal pairs of bisyllabic coordinative compounds with reversible syllable positions were examined for acoustic evidence of asymmetrical prominence relations. Clear evidence of asymmetric prominences in coordinative compounds was found, supporting independent results obtained from an analysis of reduplicative compounds and tone sandhi in Vietnamese [Nguyễn and Ingram, 2006].

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's no-word-stress coding and with the Schiering, Bickel & Hildebrandt 2010 synthesis already held by the project (which is built on these very experiments): no lexical stress distinguishing compounds from phrases; prominence is a property of a small (disyllabic) domain. It adds the instrumental caveat that asymmetric prominence is measurable inside coordinative compounds. Which syllable is stronger is not in the abstract; Schiering et al. (p.671-672) read the Ingram & Nguyen results as final-syllable strong by default. Access: open_url (the Harvard library catalogue) is a JavaScript discovery shell with no PDF; Unpaywall is_oa=false; UQ eSpace UQ:137247 lists an a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the abstract: none of five acoustic correlates (f0 range/contour, duration, intensity, spectral slope, vowel reduction) distinguishes compounds from phrases lexically, so Vietnamese has no lexical stress contrast of that kind; disambiguation, when forced, is phrase-level juncture marking. Within bisyllabic coordinative compounds an asymmetric prominence relation does exist (direction not stated in the abstract). The abstract promises 'a reconciliation of these apparently conflicting findings on word stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Asymmetric prominence in bisyllabic coordinative compounds and (per the cited 2006 work) in reduplications with tone sandhi.
new_statements.identity_note: Barker 1966 describes the six-tone system of Tonkinese (Bắc Việt, Northern Vietnamese) and notes in footnote 4 that other dialects (which include the Southern variety this entry is named for) merge hỏi and ngã into a five-tone system. Barker 1969 follows Lê Văn Lý's six-tone analysis without naming a dialect. Nguyễn & Ingram 2007a's abstract names no dialect; the abstract of its 2006 Speech Prosody precursor (UQ eSpace UQ:34b6e70, saved) states that its 45 speakers came from Hanoi, Huế and Saigon, so the compound/phrase stress result is pan-dialectal rather than specifically Southern.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Reviews the views (Emeneau: equal energy on every syllable; Thompson: three degrees, phrasal; Cao 1978: stress by syntactic relation) and asserts, citing her own unpublished ms., that 'Vietnamese appears to be an iambic language, i.e., each foot consists of a weak syllable followed by a strong one (Pham, ms)'; the paper's own evidence is clitic reduction (tone survives, segments delete), argued to show a prosodic word exists; explicitly does 'not attempt to account for stress patterns'. Impressionistic, no measurements; this is one of the iambic claims Brunelle 2017 tested and rejected.

sources.quote: Thus, it appears that local changes in the f0 as we know them from stress accent languages such as English and German, appear to play a role in the expression of focus in Vietnamese. sources.note: Pilot production/perception study of focus marking (Hanoi speakers): focus is expressed prosodically (f0, duration, amplitude trade-off) with no focus particles.
